title: Saudi Arabia and Israel: Houthi Fire, a Failed Pact and Trump's Push Test Riyadh
excerpt: Netanyahu offered to join strikes on the Houthis and was refused in public, even as quiet Saudi-Israeli consultation grows — normalisation still hinges on Palestinian statehood.
body:
• Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the failure of Riyadh's Pakistan-Turkiye defence pact to produce battlefield help, and US pressure under President Donald Trump are together reviving the question of Saudi-Israel normalisation, India Today reports.
  • Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought Saudi approval, through US mediation, for Israel to join strikes on the Houthis — Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman rejected direct Israeli participation, fearing a public backlash.
  • Saudi officials have quietly consulted Israeli officers, according to the Soufan Center, but Riyadh publicly insists normalisation still requires an irreversible pathway to Palestinian statehood.
  • No deal is imminent: the shift so far is quiet security consultation under fire, not open diplomatic recognition.

Is Saudi Arabia warming up to Israel? The pressures pushing Riyadh in that direction are real and accumulating: a Houthi campaign that has struck Saudi cities and airports, defence partners who have declined to fight alongside the kingdom, and a US president who has long wanted a Saudi-Israel deal under the Abraham Accords. Yet the evidence so far points to quiet consultation, not normalisation — and Riyadh continues to say so publicly.

The catalyst: a war Riyadh is fighting largely alone

The Houthis have advanced along Yemen's Red Sea coast, seized the port of Mokha and Red Sea islands, and taken control of Yemen's side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, through which roughly 12 percent of global trade passes, according to The Business Standard. Missile and drone strikes have hit Saudi targets repeatedly, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh; one ballistic missile strike killed at least 12 people and injured 309.

Saudi Arabia's alternative security architecture has not delivered. The Mecca Agreement with Pakistan and Turkiye contains a mutual-defence commitment, but neither partner has intervened militarily in Yemen, the Soufan Center's IntelBrief notes; Pakistani officials have argued the Yemen fighting predates the pact. The United States, seeking to avoid expanding its war with Iran, has also declined direct intervention, while providing intelligence support and clearing a sale of up to 48 F-35 fighters.

Israel knocks — and is kept at arm's length

Into that gap stepped Israel, the one regional state willing to help. Netanyahu sought Saudi approval, via US mediation, for Israel to join military operations against the Houthis — an outreach aimed both at counter-Houthi operations and at advancing formal ties. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman rejected direct Israeli participation over concerns about public backlash inside the kingdom.

The Soufan Center reports a more ambiguous picture beneath the refusal: Saudi officials have quietly consulted Israeli military officers, drawing on Israel's experience bombing Houthi targets. But a Saudi source told Israel's Kan radio that the crisis would not change Riyadh's position, and that the kingdom continues to demand an "irreversible pathway" to Palestinian statehood before normalisation. Netanyahu condemned the airport attack as a "horrific terrorist attack" and offered condolences — public signalling that costs Riyadh nothing and commits it to nothing.

Trump's long-standing push

President Donald Trump has repeatedly promoted Saudi-Israel normalisation under the Abraham Accords framework. A deal appeared close in late 2023 before Hamas's October 7 attack and the Gaza war derailed it. Washington now has fresh leverage: Riyadh needs American help it is not fully getting, and Israeli involvement against the Houthis is one of the few offers on the table.

What to watch

For the large Indian workforce in Saudi Arabia and across the Gulf, the stakes are practical: Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure are a direct safety concern, and any Saudi-Israel realignment would redraw the region's security map. The honest reading of the current evidence is narrower than the headline question suggests. Shared enemies and American pressure are producing consultation and signalling. Normalisation, on Riyadh's own stated terms, still runs through Palestinian statehood — and that condition has not moved.
